opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be back.

I think the main issue is that "AGI" was always a slightly fuzzy concept, and the way AI has actually developed has made the fuzziness much more consequential. When people first started forecasting it, the implicit picture was something like a single system that crosses a threshold and becomes roughly as capable as a human across the board, at roughly the same moment in every domain. That picture made it a natural milestone: before it, AI is a tool; after it, the world changes.

What we've actually seen is very uneven, or "jagged," capability. Current systems are superhuman at some things, like breadth of knowledge, speed, and certain kinds of coding or exam-style reasoning, while still being surprisingly weak at others, like reliably carrying out long multi-step tasks, knowing what they don't know, or learning continually on the job the way a new employee would. So if you ask "when will we have AGI?", different people will give wildly different answers, not because they disagree about the facts but because they weigh those dimensions differently. Some would say we're more or less there already; others would say we're still a long way off. That's a sign the term isn't carving reality at the joints.

The second problem is that AGI isn't really what we care about. We care about particular capabilities that drive particular consequences. For example: when can AI systems substantially automate AI research itself, which could produce a rapid feedback loop? When can they do most economically valuable remote work? When could they meaningfully help someone build a dangerous weapon, or act autonomously in ways that are hard to oversee? Those thresholds could arrive at quite different times, and some of the most important ones might come before anything people would comfortably call AGI. Others might come after.

So I'd rather forecast those specific, decision-relevant milestones, and also pay attention to the trends underneath them, like how long a task a system can complete autonomously, how costs are scaling, and how much progress is coming from scaling training versus scaling up compute at inference time. Those give you something you can actually measure and plan around. "AGI" is still a useful word for gesturing at the broad transition, but as a single date to put on a forecast, I think it now obscures more than it reveals.

r001.rationale: The response says some people consider current systems more or less to be AGI while others think AGI is still a long way off, attributing the disagreement to how they weigh different capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the main problem is that "AGI" was always a bit of a placeholder. When people started using the term, the idea was to point at something that wasn't narrow AI — a system that could do the full range of cognitive tasks a human could, rather than just play chess or recognise faces. And that was a useful contrast when the systems we had were extremely narrow. But now we've got systems that are, in a sense, already quite general. You can ask a frontier language model about almost anything and it will have a go, and often a pretty good go. So the "generality" part of the milestone has sort of arrived, and yet it doesn't feel like we've crossed the threshold that people had in mind when they talked about AGI.

What that reveals, I think, is that generality was never really the thing we cared about. It was a proxy. What people were actually pointing at was something more like: when does AI become able to do the things that matter for transforming the world? And those things come apart. One of them is whether AI can do most economically valuable work — can it actually replace human labour across the economy? Another is whether it can do AI research itself and start accelerating its own development. Another is whether it can act autonomously over long time horizons, running a project for weeks or months rather than answering a single query. Another is whether it's superhuman at things like persuasion, or cyber capabilities, or scientific discovery. These are quite different capabilities with quite different implications, and they're likely to arrive at different times.

So when you bundle them all into one word and ask "when will AGI arrive?", you end up with these conversations where people are talking past each other. One person says we already have it, another says it's decades away, and they're both sort of right because they mean different things. And for forecasting, that's really unhelpful, because the whole point of forecasting is to be able to say what we expect to happen and then check whether we were right. If the term is so fuzzy that we can't even agree whether it's been met, it's not doing its job.

The other issue is that the single-milestone framing encourages a kind of discontinuous picture — before AGI, after AGI — as though there's one moment where everything changes. I think the reality is more like a series of thresholds being crossed over a period of years, each with its own consequences. Some of them might be very dramatic. The point where AI systems can substantially accelerate AI research is one I'd single out as especially important, because that's where you could get the feedback loops that make everything else happen faster. But that's a specific, measurable thing, and I'd rather we forecast that directly than ask when we'll reach some undefined general milestone.

So my suggestion is really just to disaggregate. Pick the specific capabilities that would actually change the strategic situation, define them clearly enough that we could tell when they've arrived, and forecast those. That's harder and less catchy than "AGI by 2030," but I think it's where the real action is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says one person may think current AI already qualifies as AGI while another thinks it is decades away, and that both are “sort of right” because they mean different things.

astra-6.text:
I think the problem is that AGI has come to mean several different things, and those things may happen at quite different times. You might mean a system that can perform a very broad range of intellectual tasks, or one that can do everything a human can do, or one that could replace humans in most economically valuable work. Those aren’t the same milestone.

We’ve also tended to imagine a fairly smooth progression towards human-level intelligence, followed by a progression beyond it. But what we’re seeing is much more uneven: systems that are extraordinarily capable at some things and surprisingly poor at others. So asking when they’ll be “human level” doesn’t necessarily pick out a clear moment—or the moment we should care most about.

For forecasting, I’d rather ask about the particular capability that matters. When could AI substantially accelerate AI research? When could it carry out a long, complicated project with little supervision? When could it pose a threat that we couldn’t adequately control? Those questions still involve uncertainty, but they connect the forecast to the consequences we’re trying to understand. We shouldn’t assume that all of those consequences wait for a single threshold called AGI.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI has several meanings and describes uneven capabilities, but does not state that reasonable people can disagree about whether current AI models qualify as AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AGI bundles together a few different ideas that we should pull apart. One is whether a system can perform a very broad range of tasks. Another is how well it can perform them. And a third is what the consequences are going to be. Those don’t necessarily arrive at the same moment.

You could have a system that is very general, but is still worse than a human at a lot of important things. Or you could have systems that are quite uneven — superhuman in some areas and surprisingly poor in others — which nevertheless have enormous economic effects, or pose very serious risks. So asking when we get AGI can obscure the thing we actually want to know.

I’d rather ask about more specific milestones. When can AI substantially accelerate AI research? When can it carry out long, complicated projects with very little human supervision? When might we lose the ability to keep these systems under control? Those are distinct questions, and the answers could be quite far apart. The label ‘AGI’ makes it sound as though there’s one threshold that settles all of them.

r001.rationale: The response argues that AGI combines distinct capabilities and consequences, but it does not say whether current AI models qualify as AGI is open to reasonable disagreement.
